visualMetaphor: a merchant's ledger column that doubles every nine lines
title: The 500-year-old shortcut for doubling money
angle: Pacioli's own 1494 example is 8 percent doubling in 9 years, the same numbers investors quote today; the exact answer is 9.006.
script: How long does it take money to double? Lenders have used a shortcut for over five hundred years, and you can do it in your head. It shows up in a book printed in Venice in 1494: Luca Pacioli's Summa de arithmetica. Pacioli set it down as a rule of thumb for merchants lending at interest. He gave no proof, only the rule. Divide seventy two by the yearly interest rate, compounded once a year. The answer is roughly how many years the money takes to double. At six percent, that's twelve years. Pacioli's own example was eight percent: seventy two over eight is nine. A thousand dollars becomes about two thousand in nine years, four thousand in eighteen, and eight thousand in twenty seven. Every nine years, it doubles again. Is it accurate? The rule says nine years. The exact answer is nine point zero zero six. Close enough to do in your head. It's an estimate, not a promise. It works best between three and twelve percent. Seventy two over the rate. Five centuries old, and still the quickest way to see what time does to money.

visualMetaphor: a subscription book where a maid's hundred guilders sit two lines above a director's twelve thousand
title: The first shares anyone could buy
angle: The VOC locked investors' money in for ten years, so the only way out was to sell your share to someone else, and that is how a stock market started: trading began the day the books closed.
script: Amsterdam, August 1602. For one month, a new company let anyone in the Dutch Republic buy a piece of it. It was the Dutch East India Company. Its charter ran 21 years, and your money stayed in for at least ten. In Amsterdam alone, 1,143 investors signed up. A maid, Neeltgen Cornelis, put in 100 guilders. Each of the six directors put in 12,000. By the end, Amsterdam's book held about 3.7 million guilders. There was a catch. Once your money went in, there was no way to take it out. So you sold your share. Buyer and seller went to the East India House. Two directors approved, and the bookkeeper moved the share to the buyer's account. The oldest share we still have is a receipt from 1606. A city messenger in Enkhuizen paid 150 guilders for it. Trading began as soon as the books closed. Dividends followed from 1609, and in 1611 Amsterdam opened an Exchange building. It is the same deal behind a share today. The company keeps the money. You sell your piece to someone who wants in.

visualMetaphor: John Adams's own 1600 copy of Littleton, the camera creeping down a black-letter page until it reaches the words a dead pledge
title: Why a mortgage is a dead pledge
angle: The famous explanation, that the land is dead to the borrower if he fails to pay, is a later lawyers' reading; in 1189 a dead pledge meant one whose rents went to the lender without paying down the debt.
script: Every mortgage is named after a dead pledge. This law book from 1600 says so. In Latin, mortuum vadium. In English, a dead pledge. Mort is Old French for dead. Gage means pledge. So why would a loan be dead? The page gives a reason. If the borrower failed to pay on the day, the land was gone from him for ever. In its example, the borrower pledges land and must repay 20 pounds by a set day. Pay, and it comes back. Miss it, and the land is lost. But that reason came later. In 1189, Glanville's law book used the name for a different deal. The lender held the land and took its rents, but the rents never cut the debt. That was a dead pledge. When the rents paid the debt down, it was a living pledge, working for the borrower. Under Christian bans on profit from lending, a dead pledge counted as a kind of usury. Glanville named the dead pledge in 1189. By Littleton's Tenures, in 1481, the borrower kept the land, so Littleton gave a new reason. Coke followed it. Dead first meant rents that never cut the debt. Later it meant the land a borrower loses.

visualMetaphor: a goatskin IOU whose margins fill with 295 years of interest receipts until a paper sheet has to carry the rest
title: The loan that will never be repaid
angle: Everyone repeats that a 1648 bond still pays Yale; the twist is that it was signed the day the Dutch swore peace with Spain, kept paying through the Netherlands' own default in 1810, and today pays about 11 euros a year that someone must collect in person.
script: This IOU is 378 years old, and it still pays interest. It was signed on 15 May 1648, the day Spain and the Dutch swore peace. The borrower wasn't a king. It was a water board near Utrecht, borrowing 1,000 guilders to build piers in the river Lek. The bond has no end date. It promised 5% a year, every year, forever. Every payment was written on the goatskin itself. Later the rate was cut in half. Then the goatskin ran out of room, so in 1944 a paper sheet was added. Even its own country defaulted on its debts. In 1810 the Dutch state stopped paying, but the water board kept paying. In 2003, Yale bought the bond. There was one problem. Interest had to be collected in person. So a Yale professor took the bond over and collected 26 years at once. In 2015 a curator collected 12 more. Inflation took its toll. Today it pays just 11.35 euros a year. And the loan itself? It will never be paid back. So who won: the lender or the borrower?

visualMetaphor: a correspondent's handwritten ledger of what the neighbors said, its lines turning into a single three-digit number
title: Before your credit score, your neighbors
angle: Everyone knows the FICO score; almost no one knows it replaced 150 years of local informants writing down what the neighbors said, from Lewis Tappan's 1841 Mercantile Agency to the Retail Credit Company files Congress reined in in 1970.
script: Critics said the company behind your credit report once filed rumors about people's marriages. It's called Equifax. And it all started with your neighbors. In 1841, Lewis Tappan, a merchant who failed in the panic of 1837, founded the Mercantile Agency. Locals reported on their neighbors: was he of fair character, with good business habits? One 1855 entry calls a man without a $ in the world. Another, a rough and ready Irishman. Every name got a grade, from A plus, $1,000,000 or more, down to K: less than $2,000. Next came shoppers. In 1899, the Woolford brothers started the Retail Credit Company in Atlanta, selling notes on shoppers' payment habits. That company became Equifax. In 1970, Congress passed a credit reporting law. In the 1970s, the government accused Retail Credit of rating its staff by how much negative information they found on consumers. Then in 1989 came FICO: one number, 300 to 850. Even FICO says many of those old opinions carried racial, class and gender biases. So which would you trust: a number or your neighbors?
